title: Load Balancing and Request Routing
summary: Explain the static occupancy bounds behind two-choice routing and their limits for dynamic serving queues.

blocks.md:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Explain the static occupancy bounds behind two-choice routing and their limits for dynamic serving queues
- Explain the role of consistent hashing in maintaining KV cache session affinity and minimizing cache invalidation during fleet scaling
- Differentiate between process liveness probes, readiness checks, and deep inference health checks in GPU serving fleets
- Calculate capacity-proportional routing weights to balance resource utilization across heterogeneous accelerator fleets
- Identify the circuit breaker pattern as the primary mechanism for preventing cascading failures in inference clusters

blocks.source: Vol II, Serving at Scale, § Load Balancing and Request Routing
blocks.md: Suppose ten model replicas are serving traffic when a request for a 5,000-word document summary arrives. Assigning it to an overloaded replica adds waiting and can increase interference for work already admitted there. The effect depends on admission, batching, and priority policies. Round-robin assignment does not inspect those differences in remaining work. A state-aware router uses memory and queue information to choose a feasible destination, while limiting the cost and staleness of its observations.

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md:
In the book this section runs through:

- Tail latency under fan-out
- Round-robin and random assignment
- The power of two choices
- Weighted and adaptive load balancing
- Least-connections load balancing
- Consistent hashing for stateful routing

Pay attention to: Balls-into-bins and Power of Two Choices load balancing; Capacity-weighted routing in heterogeneous GPU fleets; Least-connections vs round-robin under high output length variance; Consistent hashing for KV cache session affinity.

blocks.prompt: Think first: Explain why Consistent Hashing is critical for routing multi-turn LLM conversations, and describe what happens to KV cache state when an autoscaling event adds a new replica.
blocks.md: When a service retains session KV state across turns, routing affinity avoids rebuilding that context. Adding a node to a balanced consistent-hash ring remaps roughly 1/(N+1) of keys from N existing nodes. Their old cache state does not move automatically: affected sessions need transfer or reconstruction, while other mappings stay stable. A stateless API supplying full history can operate without this affinity.

questions.q: Why does the power-of-two-choices result motivate probing two replicas, and what limitation applies when using the classical balls-into-bins bounds to predict a 1,000-server serving fleet?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. The cited asymptotic bounds describe equal jobs placed into initially empty bins without departures. They motivate the low coordination cost of two choices, but cannot predict a two-request production queue. Serving also depends on arrivals, service times, hardware capacity, and cached state; probes should compare normalized remaining work and be validated under the actual workload.
questions.hint: Think about: explain the static occupancy bounds behind two-choice routing and their limits for dynamic serving queues.
options: It eliminates all network packet headers by broadcasting requests to all 1,000 servers simultaneously.
Two probes improve static occupancy scaling from $\Theta(\log R/\log\log R)$ to $\Theta(\log\log R)$, but do not determine production queue depths or P99 latency
It guarantees zero queuing delay by dynamically compiling new CUDA kernels on the fly for each request.
It forces all requests to execute on CPU fallback nodes whenever GPU utilization exceeds 50%.

questions.q: Standard HTTP 200 process liveness checks are sufficient to detect GPU inference degradation caused by thermal throttling or silent HBM memory pool exhaustion.
questions.explanation: False. Process-level HTTP liveness checks only confirm that the web server daemon is running. A GPU experiencing thermal throttling, corrupted memory modules, unallocated KV pools, or un-warmed model weights will continue returning HTTP 200 while failing or stalling on real inference queries. Production fleets require Tiered Probing, specifically Deep Health checks that execute lightweight test inference requests and validate logit output distributions.
questions.hint: Think about: differentiate between process liveness probes, readiness checks, and deep inference health checks in GPU serving fleets.

questions.q: A heterogeneous inference cluster contains 10 H100 servers (delivering 1,000 QPS capacity each) and 20 A100 servers (delivering 600 QPS capacity each), serving a total target load of 15,000 QPS. What weighted routing ratio should be applied to achieve equal utilization across all hardware tiers?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. Total cluster capacity is $(10 \times 1{,}000) + (20 \times 600) = 10{,}000 + 12{,}000 = 22{,}000\text{ QPS}$. Capacity-proportional routing assigns each H100 server a weight of \$1{,}000 / 22{,}000 \approx 4.55\%$ (\$681.8\text{ QPS}$ load, \$68.2\%$ utilization) and each A100 server a weight of \$600 / 22{,}000 \approx 2.73\%$ (\$409.1\text{ QPS}$ load, \$68.2\%$ utilization). Equal routing leaves less latency headroom on the A100s (\$83.3\%$ utilization) than on H100s (\$50\%$ utilization). Both remain below their stated service capacities; these utilization values alone establish neither overload nor a tail-SLO violation.
questions.hint: Think about: calculate capacity-proportional routing weights to balance resource utilization across heterogeneous accelerator fleets.
options: Route 500 QPS equally to every server regardless of type, producing 50% utilization on H100 and 83.3% on A100.
Assign weight 1.0 to H100 and 1.0 to A100 so all servers receive equal traffic shares.
Assign capacity-proportional weights (H100 weight $= 1000/22000 \approx 4.55\%$ per server; A100 weight $= 600/22000 \approx 2.73\%$ per server), achieving uniform 68.2% utilization across all nodes.
Route 100% of traffic to A100 servers first and overflow remaining traffic to H100 servers.

questions.q: An autoregressive LLM must retain state during active decoding, but a serving API can still be stateless across completed requests if each new request supplies the required conversation history.
questions.explanation: True. The active decode loop uses per-request KV state. Retaining that state across turns is a serving choice that can save prefill work and favor routing affinity; a full-history request can instead rebuild it on another replica.
questions.hint: Think about: distinguish active autoregressive state from optional session-cache retention across requests.
